newsitem.title: FRANCE: Perissich says ordered extra BSE studies in 1993.
newsitem.headline: Perissich says ordered extra BSE studies in 1993.

text.p: Ricardo Perissich, the commission's former director general of industry, said on Monday he ordered in 1993 extra scientific studies on whether bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) could be transmitted to people.

Answering questions from the European Parliament's committee of inquiry into BSE, Perissich said he disagreed with his counterpart for agriculture, Guy Legras, over the risk that BSE might be passed to humans in the form of Creutzfeldt Jakob Disease (CJD).
Legras was said to have argued that scientific research had not revealed cause for alarm and that reopening the debate would shake public confidence and undermine the beef market.
"I did not share his opinion. I decided to call for extra studies," Perissich said, adding he had two exchanges of letters with Legras on the issue in 1993.
But Perissich, who left the Commission in 1994, added that his studies reached similar conclusions to previous research and did not justify taking extra measures.

However Italian Union for Europe MEP, Giacomo Santini, quoted Commission figures showing 77 confirmed CJD cases in 1993, including eight in Austria which only joined the EU in 1995, plus 45 deaths in Britain.
Britain gave figures for only the total number of confirmed and suspected CJD deaths. Belgium only gave figures for the flemish community.
The figures, which were gathered by the directorate general for social affairs, showed that 1993 was the peak year in the period between 1990 and 1995.
There were 31 CJD deaths in Britain but zero cases in other member states in 1990 while there were 43 deaths in Britain and 50 confirmed cases in other member states in 1995.
During the first quarter of 1996, there were 11 CJD deaths in Britain and nine confirmed cases elsewhere in the EU.
The table did not specify figures for the new CJD variant which attacks mainly young people.
